chapter: Dances and bands of his youth
title: Dance music of the Charleston era; ragtime evolved into jazz
summary: Dance bands played popular tunes of the day, with dances taking names from the music. He sees ragtime-to-jazz as evolution and refers to Souchon, Menville and Kennedy as the experts.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: the party generally tended to have jazz bands, a ragtime

ball. Well, I had the ragtime band, yeah. What about when you were in college? What kind of band was that? Well, like I say, I wasn't a great party hound, so I'm not in a position to give you any expert information. But when they had the dance houses, they'd hire a band. They would play the popular music of the day, and the popular music of the day. Well, back in the days of Charleston, they played a piece called Charlton Ta-da, I don't know if anything goes. And the Black Bottom and all those kind of things. Well, the music went with the song, I mean the dance. The dance took its name back to the music. They were collateral relatives. But actually, my recollection is that the whole thing has been just an evolutionary process. It went from ragtime into jazz. Just what the difference is, the jazz musicologists like Sue and Edmond Souchon and Myra Menville and Goop Kennedy knows quite a bit about it.
